questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Layer the primitive streak develops in
questions.question: The primitive streak develops in which layer of embryonic disc?

explanations.A: Correct. The primitive streak appears at the beginning of the third week as a linear thickening within the epiblast, formed by the proliferation and migration of epiblast cells toward the disc's midline. It is the epiblast, not the hypoblast, that goes on to give rise to all three definitive germ layers, since epiblast cells ingress through the streak to displace the hypoblast (forming endoderm) and to form the intraembryonic mesoderm, leaving the remaining epiblast as the ectoderm. Because every later germ layer traces back to this single epiblast population, the primitive streak's location in the epiblast is the starting point for the whole of gastrulation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The hypoblast is displaced by ingressing epiblast cells rather than contributing to the primitive streak itself; it does not persist as endoderm, a common point of confusion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mesoderm is a product that the primitive streak generates once epiblast cells migrate through it, not the layer the streak itself develops within.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Endoderm, like mesoderm, is a downstream product of gastrulation through the primitive streak, not its site of origin.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The notochord forms from cells passing through the primitive node at the streak's cranial end, a related but distinct structure from the streak itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that the primitive streak develops within the epiblast.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure derived from somites
questions.question: Which of the following is derived from Somites:

explanations.A: Correct. Each somite splits into a ventromedial sclerotome, which forms the vertebrae, and a dorsolateral dermomyotome, which further divides into a dermatome and a myotome. The dermatome portion gives rise to the dermis of the skin over most of the body, so dermis is a genuine somite derivative alongside the axial skeleton and skeletal muscle. This dermatome/myotome/sclerotome split is the standard framework these somite-derivative questions are built around.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sensory, sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia are neural crest derivatives, not somite derivatives; the neural crest arises separately from the neural folds rather than from the paraxial mesoderm.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The pleura is a lateral plate mesoderm derivative (from the somatic and splanchnic layers lining the coelom), not a somite derivative.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lungs are an endodermal outgrowth of the foregut for their epithelium, with mesenchyme from the surrounding splanchnic mesoderm; neither component traces to the somites.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The kidneys develop from the intermediate mesoderm, a separate intraembryonic mesoderm column from the paraxial mesoderm that forms somites.

questions.learning_objective: State that the dermis of the skin is a somite (dermatome) derivative.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 2 (a, remark: "Dermis develop from somites.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Syndrome with 44+XXY chromosomes (i)
questions.question: Which syndrome has 44 XXY chromosomes?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Down syndrome is trisomy 21, an extra copy of an autosome (chromosome 21), giving a formula such as 45+XY or 45+XX, not a sex-chromosome aneuploidy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Turner syndrome is a monosomy of the sex chromosomes, 44+XO (45,X), the opposite pattern from an extra sex chromosome.
explanations.C: Correct. Klinefelter (Kleinfelter) syndrome is a trisomy of the sex chromosomes, 44+XXY (47,XXY), arising when an ovum carrying two X chromosomes, produced by non-disjunction in the first meiotic division of the oocyte, is fertilised by a Y-bearing sperm. Affected males are typically tall, with small testes, reduced fertility, and sometimes gynaecomastia, and carry a single Barr body from their extra X chromosome. This 44+XXY formula is the single most frequently repeated chromosomal fact across this exam bank.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Edward syndrome is trisomy 18, another autosomal trisomy, not a sex-chromosome aneuploidy.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cri du chat syndrome is caused by a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5, a structural autosomal abnormality unrelated to sex-chromosome number.

questions.learning_objective: Name Klinefelter syndrome as the 44+XXY sex-chromosome trisomy.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 3 (c, remark: "Klienfilter syndrome.")

questions.subject: obs
questions.title: Name for cord attached to placental margin
questions.question: An umbilical cord attached to the margin of Placenta is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Velamentous insertion is when the cord inserts into the fetal membranes beyond the placental edge, leaving the vessels to run unprotected through the membranes before reaching the placenta itself, a distinct and generally riskier abnormality from a simple marginal attachment.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Placenta accreta refers to abnormal placental invasion into the myometrium, an attachment abnormality of the placenta to the uterine wall, not a cord-insertion abnormality.
explanations.C: Correct. When the umbilical cord inserts at the margin (edge) of the placental disc, rather than centrally or paracentrally, this is called battledore placenta. The name comes from its resemblance to a battledore (paddle) racket, with the handle (cord) attached at the rim. It is generally a benign variant, though it carries a modestly increased risk of fetal growth restriction and cord compression.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A succenturiate placenta has one or more accessory lobes separate from the main placental mass, connected by vessels running through the membranes, an abnormality of placental shape rather than of cord insertion site.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A false knot is a local redundancy or varicosity of umbilical vessels or Wharton's jelly that only looks like a knot, unrelated to where the cord inserts into the placenta.

questions.learning_objective: Name battledore placenta as marginal attachment of the umbilical cord.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 4 (c, remark: "Battledore placenta.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Major source of intraembryonic mesoderm
questions.question: The major source of intraembryonic mesoderm is:

explanations.A: Correct. Epiblast cells ingress through the primitive streak and spread laterally and cranially between the epiblast and hypoblast to form the bulk of the intraembryonic mesoderm; the primitive node and notochord contribute further mesoderm, but the streak is the major, and first, source. This mesoderm then splits into paraxial, intermediate and lateral plate columns, and is genuinely absent only where the oropharyngeal and cloacal membranes keep ectoderm and endoderm fused directly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ectoderm is what remains of the epiblast after cells have migrated inward through the streak; it is not itself a source of mesoderm.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Endoderm is formed by epiblast cells displacing the hypoblast, a separate ingression event from the one that generates mesoderm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The prechordal plate is a small area of tightly adherent bilaminar (ectoderm-endoderm) cells cranial to the primitive node that marks the future oropharyngeal membrane; it is one of the mesoderm-free zones, not a mesoderm source.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The neurenteric canal is a transient passage between the amniotic cavity and yolk sac formed through the primitive pit; it is not a source of mesoderm.

questions.learning_objective: State that the primitive streak is the major source of intraembryonic mesoderm.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Normal amniotic fluid volume at birth
questions.question: The normal volume of amniotic fluid at birth is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 100 mL is far below even the abnormally reduced (oligohydramnios) range; it does not represent a normal term volume.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 200 mL remains well under the normal term figure, closer to the volumes seen in oligohydramnios than to a healthy pregnancy at term.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 500 mL is closer to the normal figure but still understates it; amniotic fluid volume continues to rise toward term.
explanations.D: Correct. Amniotic fluid volume increases across gestation and normally measures approximately 1000 mL, one litre, at full term, though healthy pregnancies can vary somewhat above or below this figure. This term value is the reference exam questions use when asking for the normal volume of amniotic fluid at birth, and it sits well above the thresholds used to define oligohydramnios or polyhydramnios.
explanations.E: Incorrect. 1500 mL overstates the normal term volume and would instead be more consistent with a degree of polyhydramnios.

questions.learning_objective: State that the normal amniotic fluid volume at term is approximately 1000 mL.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 6 (d, remark: "1000 ml (1 litre).")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Syndrome caused by chromosomal monosomy
questions.question: A syndrome caused by chromosomal monosomy:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Down syndrome is caused by trisomy 21, an extra chromosome, not a missing one.
explanations.B: Correct. Turner syndrome, 44+XO (45,X), is caused by a monosomy of the sex chromosomes, arising when an ovum with no X chromosome (from non-disjunction) is fertilised by an X-bearing sperm. Affected females characteristically have no Barr body, since there is only a single X to begin with, and show short stature, limb oedema, underdeveloped ovaries and primary amenorrhoea. It is the only monosomy compatible with survival to term among the syndromes commonly listed on this kind of exam item.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome, 44+XXY, is a trisomy of the sex chromosomes, an extra chromosome rather than a missing one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Edward syndrome is trisomy 18, an autosomal trisomy, not a monosomy.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cri du chat syndrome is a structural deletion on chromosome 5, not a whole-chromosome monosomy.

questions.learning_objective: Name Turner syndrome as the sex-chromosome monosomy among the commonly listed syndromes.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 7 (b, remark: "Turner syndrome = 44+XO.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Syndrome with 44+XXY chromosomes (ii)
questions.question: Which of the following syndromes has the genotype 44 + XXY?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Down syndrome's genotype is a trisomy of an autosome (chromosome 21, e.g. 45+XY), not a sex-chromosome trisomy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Turner syndrome's genotype is 44+XO, a monosomy, the opposite of an extra sex chromosome.
explanations.C: Correct. Klinefelter syndrome's genotype is 44+XXY, a trisomy of the sex chromosomes arising from non-disjunction in oogenesis followed by fertilisation with a Y-bearing sperm. This is the same fact tested from a different distractor set elsewhere in this bank, underscoring how frequently the Klinefelter=44+XXY pairing recurs across this exam's chromosomal-syndrome items.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Superfemale (triple X) syndrome's genotype is 44+XXX, an extra X but without a Y, not the XXY combination.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Edward syndrome's genotype is a trisomy of chromosome 18 (e.g. 45+XY), an autosomal rather than a sex-chromosome trisomy.

questions.learning_objective: Name Klinefelter syndrome as the 44+XXY sex-chromosome trisomy, distinguishing it from Turner and superfemale.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Intraembryonic mesoderm part forming the kidneys
questions.question: The kidneys are derived from which part of the intraembryonic mesoderm?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cranial somites, like all somites, arise from paraxial mesoderm and form the axial skeleton, dermis and skeletal muscle, not the kidneys.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Caudal somites share the same paraxial-mesoderm origin and fate as cranial somites; neither region of the somite column forms the urinary system.
explanations.C: Correct. The intermediate mesoderm, also called the intermediate cell mass or nephrogenic cord, is the intraembryonic mesoderm column between the paraxial and lateral plate columns, and it gives rise to the urogenital system, including the kidneys and gonads. This three-way subdivision of intraembryonic mesoderm, paraxial, intermediate and lateral plate, is the framework every 'which mesoderm forms X' question in this cluster is testing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The visceral (splanchnic) layer of lateral plate mesoderm contributes to the wall of the gut tube and to the heart, not to the kidneys.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The somatic (parietal) layer of lateral plate mesoderm contributes to the body wall and limb connective tissue, not to the kidneys.

questions.learning_objective: State that the kidneys develop from the intermediate mesoderm (intermediate cell mass).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 9 (c, remark: "Intermediate cell mass.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure derived from ectoderm
questions.question: Derived from ectoderm:

explanations.A: Incorrect per standard teaching (and per this option's own printed remark). The adrenal cortex develops from mesoderm (coelomic epithelium/intermediate mesoderm), not ectoderm.
explanations.B: Incorrect per standard teaching. The dura mater is a mesodermal derivative, not an ectodermal one.
explanations.C: The standard-teaching correct answer, though not the letter the source prints for this row. Melanocytes are neural crest cells, and the neural crest is itself an ectodermal derivative (it separates from the ectodermal neural folds as they fuse), so melanocytes are the one option on this list that is genuinely ectodermal in origin.
explanations.D: Incorrect per standard teaching. The dermis of the skin is a mesodermal derivative (from the dermatome), while only the epidermis above it is ectodermal.
explanations.E: Printed as correct in the source key, though this conflicts with standard teaching. The heart is a mesodermal derivative (from the splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm via the cardiogenic area), not an ectodermal one; the printed key's own remark reads "Pia matter," which is not even one of this question's five options. The letter is retained here per house rule (printed keys stand), but this row is very likely a genuine error in the source bank -- flagged for a human reviewer, with melanocyte (option C) noted as the standard-teaching answer.

questions.learning_objective: Identify melanocytes as the standard-teaching ectodermal (neural crest) derivative among adrenal cortex, dura mater, dermis and heart.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure not found in the full-term umbilical cord
questions.question: Which of the following is not found in the umbilical cord at full term:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS found in the cord at term). The full-term cord normally retains both umbilical arteries.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS found in the cord at term). Wharton's jelly is the mucous connective tissue that gives the cord its bulk and protects its vessels throughout gestation.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this IS found in the cord at term). The left umbilical vein is the one member of the original vein pair that persists to term, carrying oxygenated blood from the placenta to the fetus.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this IS found in the cord at term, as a remnant). The allantois projects into the connecting stalk early in development and its remnant persists within the cord, even though it is functionally regressed by term.
explanations.E: Correct. The umbilical cord originally contains a pair of umbilical veins as well as a pair of umbilical arteries, but the right umbilical vein normally degenerates during the embryonic period, leaving only the left umbilical vein at full term. So the right umbilical vein is the one structure on this list genuinely absent from the normal full-term cord, distinguishing it from the two arteries, Wharton's jelly and the allantoic remnant, all of which are normally present.

questions.learning_objective: State that the right umbilical vein, unlike the right and left umbilical arteries, does not persist to full term.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 11 (e, remark: "Left umbilical vein.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Part of the skin that is mesodermal
questions.question: Which part of the skin is mesodermal in origin?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The epidermis is ectodermal, forming the skin's outer, avascular epithelial layer.
explanations.B: Correct. The dermis, the connective-tissue layer beneath the epidermis that gives the skin its structural support and carries its blood vessels, develops from mesoderm, specifically the dermatome portion of the somites over most of the body. This is the one mesodermal component among the skin structures listed here; every other option is ectodermal, either directly (epidermis and its keratinised appendages) or via the neural crest (pigment cells).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Nails are epidermal appendages, ectodermal in origin like the epidermis they grow from.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hairs, like nails, are ectodermal epidermal appendages.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Pigment cells (melanocytes) are neural crest cells that migrate into the epidermis; the neural crest is itself an ectodermal derivative, so melanocytes are ectodermal in lineage despite arriving in the epidermis from elsewhere.

questions.learning_objective: State that the dermis, unlike the epidermis and its appendages, is mesodermal in origin.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 12 (b, remark: "Dermis of skin is mesodermal.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Origin of the lining of respiratory passages
questions.question: The lining of respiratory passages is derived from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Surface ectoderm gives rise to the epidermis and its appendages, not the internal epithelial lining of the airway.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Neural crest gives rise to peripheral neural and pigment structures, not the respiratory epithelium.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mesoderm forms the cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue that surround the respiratory passages, but not their epithelial lining itself.
explanations.D: Correct. The respiratory system arises as a ventral outgrowth (the laryngotracheal diverticulum) of the endodermal foregut, so the epithelium lining the pharynx, trachea, bronchial tree and alveoli is endodermal, the same germ layer that lines the rest of the gut tube. The surrounding cartilage, smooth muscle and connective tissue of these structures are mesodermal, but the question specifically asks about the lining.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Neuroectoderm gives rise to the central nervous system, not the respiratory tract's epithelial lining.

questions.learning_objective: State that the epithelial lining of the respiratory passages is endodermal in origin.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 13 (d, remark: "Endoderm.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Fetal anomaly suggested by oligohydramnios (i)
questions.question: The presence of oligohydramnios suggests the presence of which fetal anomaly?

explanations.A: Correct. From the second trimester onward, fetal urine production is the dominant source of amniotic fluid, so bilateral renal agenesis, in which the kidneys fail to form at all, is the classic cause of oligohydramnios, an abnormally reduced amniotic fluid volume. Severe oligohydramnios from this cause is itself dangerous, since it compresses the fetus and can restrict lung development.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Esophageal atresia prevents the fetus from swallowing amniotic fluid, and so is instead the classic cause of the opposite finding, polyhydramnios.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Maternal diabetes is a recognised cause of polyhydramnios (through fetal polyuria from hyperglycaemia), not oligohydramnios.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Like esophageal atresia, intestinal obstruction blocks fluid from being swallowed and absorbed, producing polyhydramnios rather than oligohydramnios.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Pyloric stenosis, a postnatal condition of infancy, is not a classic prenatal cause of oligohydramnios; even as a fetal GI obstruction it would tend toward polyhydramnios rather than oligohydramnios.

questions.learning_objective: State that oligohydramnios classically suggests fetal renal agenesis.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 14 (a, remark: "Renal agenesis causes oligohydramnios.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Syndrome with 44+XO genotype
questions.question: Which of the following syndromes has the genotype 44 + XO?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Down syndrome's genotype is a trisomy of chromosome 21, not a sex-chromosome monosomy.
explanations.B: Correct. Turner syndrome's genotype is 44+XO, a monosomy of the sex chromosomes arising when an ovum with no X chromosome is fertilised by an X-bearing sperm. Affected females have no Barr body, since only a single X chromosome is present, and characteristically show short stature, limb oedema and underdeveloped ovaries.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Klinefelter syndrome's genotype is 44+XXY, an extra sex chromosome, the opposite pattern from Turner's missing one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Superfemale (triple X) syndrome's genotype is 44+XXX, an extra X chromosome.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Supermale syndrome's genotype is 44+XYY, an extra Y chromosome, not a missing X.

questions.learning_objective: Name Turner syndrome as the 44+XO sex-chromosome monosomy.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 15 (b, remark: "Turner syndrome.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure derived from the paraxial mesoderm
questions.question: Derived from the paraxial mesoderm:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The spinal cord is a neural tube derivative, ectodermal in origin, not a paraxial mesoderm derivative.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cardiac muscle develops from the splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm (the cardiogenic area), not from paraxial mesoderm.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The kidneys develop from the intermediate mesoderm, a different intraembryonic mesoderm column from the paraxial mesoderm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The pleura develops from lateral plate mesoderm, which lines the coelomic cavities, not from paraxial mesoderm.
explanations.E: Correct. Paraxial mesoderm forms the somites, each of which splits into a sclerotome (forming the vertebrae) and a dermomyotome, whose dermatome portion forms the dermis of the skin over most of the body. Dermis is therefore a genuine paraxial mesoderm derivative, distinguishing it from the other four options, all of which trace to intermediate mesoderm, lateral plate mesoderm, or the neural tube instead.

questions.learning_objective: State that the dermis of the skin, unlike cardiac muscle, kidneys or pleura, is a paraxial mesoderm (somite) derivative.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 16 (e, remark: "Dermis of skin.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Number of somites at the 22nd day
questions.question: The number of somites during the 22nd day is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Two somites would fall short of the day-22 total under the standard somite/day-count relationship.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Four somites is the count for day 21, one day earlier, not day 22.
explanations.C: Correct. The first pair of somites appears on day 20 (one somite pair), and three pairs are added each day thereafter during the regular somite period, so day 21 has 1+3=4 somites and day 22 has 4+3=7 somites. This day-by-day arithmetic (age in days = (somite count-1)/3 + 20) is the same relationship the printed key spells out and that the other somite-counting items in this bank apply.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ten somites corresponds to day 23 under the same formula, one day later than day 22.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Thirteen somites would correspond to a later day still, well past day 22.

questions.learning_objective: Apply the somite-count-by-day relationship to state that day 22 corresponds to seven somites.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 17 (c, remark: "Day 20 -> 1 somite. Day 21 -> 1+3=4 somites. Day 22 -> 4+3=7 somites.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Day the anterior neuropore closes
questions.question: The anterior neuropore closes on day:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Day 15 is too early; the neural tube itself has barely begun forming by this point in the third week.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Day 18 remains before neural tube closure is underway at the level needed for the neuropores to close.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Day 21 is also too early for anterior neuropore closure.
explanations.D: Correct. The neural tube closes first in the cervical region and proceeds like a zipper toward both ends, and the anterior (cranial) neuropore, the last opening at the rostral end, closes on approximately day 25. This is a few days before the posterior neuropore closes, and failure of anterior neuropore closure underlies anencephaly.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Day 28 is closer to when the posterior neuropore closes, a few days after the anterior neuropore rather than the day the anterior one itself closes.

questions.learning_objective: State that the anterior neuropore closes on day 25.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 18 (d, remark: "Anterior neuropore closes at 25th day.")

questions.question: Klinefelter's syndrome has a genotype of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 44+XY is the normal male genotype, not Klinefelter's.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 44+XXX is the triple X (superfemale) genotype, an extra X without a Y.
explanations.C: Correct. explanations.E: Incorrect. 44+XYY is the supermale genotype, an extra Y chromosome rather than an extra X.

questions.learning_objective: State that Klinefelter syndrome's genotype is 44+XXY.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Source of the axial skeleton (i)
questions.question: The axial skeleton develops from the:

explanations.A: Correct. Paraxial mesoderm forms the somites, and each somite's ventromedial sclerotome cells migrate to surround the notochord and neural tube, going on to form the vertebrae and intervertebral discs that make up the axial skeleton. The dermomyotome portion of the same somites separately forms the dermis and skeletal muscle, but it is specifically the sclerotome that builds the axial skeleton itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Intermediate mesoderm forms the urogenital system (kidneys and gonads), not the axial skeleton.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lateral plate mesoderm forms the body-wall and limb connective tissue and the serous membrane linings, not the axial skeleton.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Surface ectoderm forms the epidermis and its appendages, unrelated to skeletal formation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Neural crest cells form the cranial (branchial-arch-derived) skeleton in part, along with peripheral neural and pigment structures, but the axial (vertebral) skeleton specifically is a paraxial mesoderm/somite derivative.

questions.learning_objective: State that the axial skeleton develops from paraxial mesoderm (via the somite sclerotomes).

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 20 (a, remark: "Paraxial mesoderm forms axial skeleton.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Location of the allantois
questions.question: The allantois is present in the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The septum transversum is a separate mesodermal structure repositioned ventrally during folding, contributing to the diaphragm and the liver's fibrous framework; it does not contain the allantois.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Chorionic villi are the finger-like projections of the developing placenta that maximise maternal-fetal exchange, a distinct structure from the allantois.
explanations.C: Correct. The allantois arises as a small diverticulum from the caudal wall of the yolk sac, in continuity with the hindgut, and extends from there into the connecting stalk, the structure that will become the umbilical cord. It is therefore anatomically located within the connecting stalk from early development onward, and its vessels go on to form the umbilical arteries and vein.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The amniotic cavity is the fluid-filled space surrounding the embryo, not the location of the allantois.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The placenta develops from chorionic villi and the decidua basalis, a separate structure from the allantois, though the allantois's vessels do go on to vascularise the placenta via the connecting stalk/umbilical cord.

questions.learning_objective: State that the allantois is located within the connecting stalk.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 22 (c, remark: "Allantois lies within connecting stalk.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure NOT derived from ectoderm
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT derived from ectoderm?

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS derived from ectoderm). The spinal cord is a neural tube derivative, ectodermal in origin.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS derived from ectoderm). The epidermis and its appendages (hair, nails, glands) are surface ectoderm derivatives.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this IS derived from ectoderm). Neural crest cells separate from the ectodermal neural folds as the neural tube closes, so the neural crest itself is an ectodermal derivative.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this IS derived from ectoderm). The sensory epithelium of specialised sense organs (ear, nose, eye) is an ectodermal derivative.
explanations.E: Correct. The adrenal (suprarenal) gland has a dual origin: its cortex arises from mesodermal cells of the intermediate mesoderm/coelomic epithelium, alongside the gonads and kidneys, while only its inner medulla is a neural crest (and so ultimately ectodermal) derivative. The adrenal cortex is therefore the one structure on this list that is genuinely NOT ectodermal, distinguishing it from its own medulla as well as from the four other, genuinely ectodermal, options.

questions.learning_objective: State that the adrenal cortex, unlike the adrenal medulla, is mesodermal rather than ectodermal in origin.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 23 (e, remark: "Adrenal cortex is mesodermal in origin.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Source of the axial skeleton (ii)
questions.question: The axial skeleton is derived from the:

explanations.A: Correct. Somites, the segmented blocks of paraxial mesoderm, each split into a sclerotome whose cells migrate to surround the notochord and neural tube and go on to form the vertebrae and intervertebral discs of the axial skeleton. This is the same fact tested from a germ-layer angle in Q20 (paraxial mesoderm), now tested by naming the structure (somites) that mesoderm forms.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The intermediate cell mass of mesoderm forms the urogenital system (kidneys and gonads), not the axial skeleton.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Intraembryonic somatopleure (somatic mesoderm plus the ectoderm it lines) contributes to the body wall, not the axial skeleton.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The neural groove is the depressed midline of the neural plate that folds to form the neural tube; it gives rise to the central nervous system, not the skeleton.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Intraembryonic splanchnopleure (splanchnic mesoderm plus the endoderm it lines) contributes to the gut wall and its associated structures, not the axial skeleton.

questions.learning_objective: State that the axial skeleton is derived from the somites.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 24 (a, remark: "Axial skeleton is derived from somites.")
field_notes.dup_check: Same underlying fact as Q20 (axial skeleton from paraxial mesoderm/somites) but a materially different, non-overlapping distractor set (Q20 tests the three mesoderm columns plus ectoderm/neural crest; Q24 tests intermediate cell mass, somatopleure, neural groove and splanchnopleure) -- kept distinct per the house distractor-difference rule.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure endodermal in origin
questions.question: Which of the following is endodermal in origin:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The brain is a neural tube derivative, ectodermal in origin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The heart develops from the splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm, a mesodermal derivative.
explanations.C: Correct. The bronchial tree arises as a ventral outgrowth (the laryngotracheal diverticulum) of the endodermal foregut, so its epithelial lining is endodermal, the same source as the rest of the gut tube's lining. The cartilage and smooth muscle surrounding that same epithelium are mesodermal, so only the lining itself, not the whole bronchial wall, is genuinely endodermal. This same endoderm-lines-the-airway fact is tested from the angle of the respiratory passages generally in Q13 and from the angle of the gastrointestinal tract in Q39.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The eye's neural components (retina) are neural tube/neuroectoderm derivatives, and its lens is a surface ectoderm derivative; neither is endodermal.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The dermis of the skin is mesodermal, derived from the dermatome portion of the somites.

questions.learning_objective: State that the bronchial tree's epithelial lining is endodermal in origin.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 25 (c, remark: "Bronchial tree is endodermal in origin.")
field_notes.dup_check: Same core fact as Q13 (respiratory lining is endodermal) but a materially different, non-overlapping distractor set (Q13 tests other germ layers/neuroectoderm; Q25 tests brain/heart/eye/dermis, a broader whole-organ derivative list) -- kept distinct per the house distractor-difference rule.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Oligohydramnios presence indicates (ii)
questions.question: Oligohydramnios could indicate the presence of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Maternal diabetes is a recognised cause of polyhydramnios, through fetal polyuria driven by maternal hyperglycaemia, not of oligohydramnios.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A true knot in the umbilical cord is a mechanical cord complication, not a recognised cause of reduced amniotic fluid volume.
explanations.C: Correct. From the second trimester onward, fetal urine is the dominant source of amniotic fluid, so bilateral renal agenesis, which abolishes fetal urine output, is the classic cause of oligohydramnios. This is the same underlying fact tested with a different distractor set in Q14, and it remains the answer exam writers reach for whenever a question asks what oligohydramnios points to. Severe oligohydramnios from this cause is itself dangerous, since it compresses the fetus and can restrict lung development.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A large-for-dates fetus is more often associated with polyhydramnios (as in maternal diabetes) or is simply unrelated to fluid volume, not a cause of oligohydramnios.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Esophageal atresia prevents the fetus from swallowing fluid, so it is the classic cause of polyhydramnios, the opposite finding from oligohydramnios.

questions.learning_objective: State that oligohydramnios classically indicates fetal renal agenesis.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 26 (c, remark: "Renal agenesis.")
field_notes.dup_check: Same underlying fact as Q14 (oligohydramnios -> renal agenesis) but a materially different, non-overlapping distractor set (Q14: renal agenesis/esophageal atresia/diabetes/intestinal obstruction/pyloric stenosis; Q26: diabetes in mother/cord knots/renal agenesis/large fetus/esophageal atresia) -- kept distinct per the house distractor-difference rule.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Drug that is NOT teratogenic
questions.question: Which of the following drugs is NOT teratogenic?

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS teratogenic). Several anticonvulsants (e.g. phenytoin, valproate) are well-established teratogens, causing recognisable fetal anticonvulsant syndromes.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS teratogenic/fetotoxic). Tetracycline crosses the placenta and deposits in developing fetal bone and teeth, causing discolouration and, with prolonged use, impaired bone growth.
explanations.C: Correct. Heparin is a large, highly charged molecule that does not cross the placental barrier in clinically significant amounts, so it is not associated with fetal malformation and is the anticoagulant of choice when anticoagulation is required during pregnancy. This distinguishes it sharply from warfarin, a small molecule that does cross the placenta and is a well-established teratogen. It is exactly this heparin-versus-everything-else contrast that questions asking which drug is NOT teratogenic are testing.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this IS teratogenic/fetotoxic). Antithyroid drugs such as methimazole and propylthiouracil cross the placenta and can cause fetal goitre or, with methimazole specifically, a recognised pattern of malformations.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this IS associated with fetal risk). Valium (diazepam) and other benzodiazepines have been linked to an increased risk of cleft lip/palate with first-trimester use and to neonatal floppy-infant/withdrawal syndromes.

questions.learning_objective: State that heparin, unlike warfarin and other listed drugs, is not teratogenic.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 28 (c, remark: "Heparin is a safe anticoagulant.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Day the embryo shows 10 pairs of somites
questions.question: At which day the embryo shows 10 pairs of somites?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Day 20 is when the first somite pair appears (one pair), far fewer than ten.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Day 21 corresponds to four somite pairs (1+3) under the standard day-by-day formula, not ten.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Day 22 corresponds to seven somite pairs (4+3), still short of ten.
explanations.D: Correct. The first somite pair appears on day 20, and three pairs are added on each subsequent day, giving 4 on day 21, 7 on day 22, and 10 on day 23. This same day-by-day arithmetic is what Q17 tests from the opposite direction (day given, count asked), and it is the standard relationship (age in days = (somite count-1)/3 + 20) this exam bank repeats across several items.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Day 24 would correspond to thirteen somite pairs (10+3) under the same formula, one step past the day with ten pairs.

questions.learning_objective: Apply the somite-count-by-day relationship to state that day 23 corresponds to ten somite pairs.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 29 (d, remark: "At day 23 -> the embryo has 10 pairs of somites.")
field_notes.dup_check: Same somite-count-by-day arithmetic as Q17, but the question direction is reversed (Q17 gives the day and asks the count; Q29 gives the count and asks the day) with a non-overlapping option set -- kept distinct per the house distractor-difference rule.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure that is ectodermal in origin
questions.question: Which of the following is ectodermal in origin:

explanations.A: Correct. The brain is part of the central nervous system, which develops entirely from the neural tube, itself formed by the folding and fusion of the ectodermal neural plate. Of the five organs listed, only the brain traces to ectoderm; the rest are mesodermal or endodermal, which is exactly the contrast this item is built to test.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The heart develops from the splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm (the cardiogenic area), a mesodermal derivative.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lung's epithelial lining is an endodermal outgrowth of the foregut, even though its surrounding mesenchyme is mesodermal.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The liver arises as an endodermal outgrowth (the hepatic diverticulum) of the foregut, with its stroma contributed by the septum transversum mesoderm.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The kidney develops from the intermediate mesoderm, a mesodermal derivative.

questions.learning_objective: State that the brain, unlike the heart, lung, liver or kidney, is ectodermal (neural tube) in origin.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 30 (a, remark: "Brain is ectodermal in origin.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Chromosomal formula of a boy with Down's syndrome
questions.question: A boy having Down's syndrome is characterized by a chromosomal formula:

explanations.A: Incorrect. 44+XO is the Turner syndrome formula, a sex-chromosome monosomy unrelated to Down syndrome's autosomal trisomy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 44+XXY is the Klinefelter syndrome formula, a sex-chromosome trisomy, not Down syndrome's autosomal trisomy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 45+XX would combine an autosomal trisomy with a female sex-chromosome pair; a boy is XY, not XX.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 43+XY understates the autosome count; Down syndrome adds an extra autosome (trisomy 21) rather than losing one, so the total autosomal count is 45, not 43.
explanations.E: Correct. Down syndrome is trisomy 21, an extra copy of chromosome 21 most often from meiotic non-disjunction, giving 45 autosomes; a boy with Down syndrome therefore has the sex-chromosome pair XY, for an overall formula of 45+XY. This is the standard way this exam bank writes a trisomy alongside a normal sex-chromosome pair, and it is the male counterpart of the 45+XX formula a girl with Down syndrome would carry.

questions.learning_objective: State that a male with Down syndrome (trisomy 21) has the chromosomal formula 45+XY.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 31 (e, remark: "Down syndrome = Trisomy 21 = 45 + XY.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Fetal abnormality indicated by hydramnios
questions.question: Hydramnios could indicate which abnormality in the fetus?

explanations.A: Correct. Hydramnios (polyhydramnios), an abnormal excess of amniotic fluid, classically results from a fetal inability to swallow and absorb the fluid it normally drinks throughout gestation, and esophageal atresia, in which the esophagus ends blindly, is the single most commonly tested cause. This is the same fact Q37 tests from a broader, category-level angle (gastrointestinal anomalies in general) rather than naming esophageal atresia specifically.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Renal agenesis abolishes fetal urine production, the major source of amniotic fluid, so it causes oligohydramnios, the opposite finding from hydramnios.
explanations.C: Incorrect. An enlarged fetal liver is not a classic cause of hydramnios; it is more typically associated with conditions such as fetal anaemia or storage disease, unrelated to fluid swallowing.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An enlarged fetal spleen is likewise not a recognised classic cause of hydramnios.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cardiac anomalies are not the classic mechanism for hydramnios; the standard teaching mechanism is a blocked swallowing/GI pathway, as in esophageal atresia.

questions.learning_objective: State that hydramnios classically indicates esophageal atresia among fetal abnormalities.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 32 (a, remark: "Hydramnios results from oesophageal atresia.")
field_notes.dup_check: Same underlying fact as Q37 (both point hydramnios to esophageal atresia/GI cause) but a materially different, non-overlapping distractor set (Q32 names specific organ anomalies; Q37 names broad anomaly categories) -- kept distinct per the house distractor-difference rule.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure derived from the intermediate cell mass
questions.question: Which of the following is derived from the intermediate cell mass of intraembryonic mesoderm?

explanations.A: Correct. The intermediate mesoderm (intermediate cell mass) is the intraembryonic mesoderm column between the paraxial and lateral plate columns, and it gives rise to the kidneys and gonads. This is the same fact Q9 tests by asking which part of the mesoderm forms the kidneys; here the question direction is reversed, naming the intermediate cell mass and asking which organ it forms.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The heart develops from the splanchnic layer of lateral plate mesoderm (the cardiogenic area), not from the intermediate mesoderm.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The dermis develops from the dermatome portion of the somites, which arise from paraxial rather than intermediate mesoderm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Trunk (skeletal) muscles develop from the myotome portion of the somites, again a paraxial mesoderm derivative.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Blood vessels develop diffusely from mesoderm generally (via vasculogenesis), not specifically from the intermediate mesoderm column.

questions.learning_objective: State that the kidneys, not the heart, dermis, trunk muscles or blood vessels, are derived from the intermediate cell mass of intraembryonic mesoderm.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 33 (a, remark: "Kidneys develop from intermediate cell mass.")
field_notes.dup_check: Same underlying fact as Q9 (kidneys <-> intermediate mesoderm) but the question direction is reversed (Q9 asks which mesoderm forms the kidneys; Q33 names the intermediate cell mass and asks which organ it forms) with a non-overlapping option set -- kept distinct per the house distractor-difference rule.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Day the earliest somites begin to appear
questions.question: The earliest somites begin to appear on day:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Day 15 is before the primitive streak itself is well established; somite formation has not yet begun.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Day 18 remains before the first somite pair forms.
explanations.C: Correct. The first pair of somites appears on approximately day 20 of development, after which three additional pairs form each day. This is the same starting point Q17 and Q29's somite-count-by-day arithmetic both build from, and it is the day this bank's own Q53 asks about again with a different (day-numbered) option set.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Day 25 is well after somites have already begun appearing; by this stage many somite pairs are already present.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Day 28 is even later, closer to when the somite period is concluding rather than beginning.

questions.learning_objective: State that the earliest somites appear on day 20 of development.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 34 (c, remark: "1st somite appears on day 20.")
field_notes.dup_check: Same day-20 fact as Q53 but a materially different, non-overlapping option set (Q34: 15/18/20/25/28; Q53: 10th/15th/20th/28th/35th) -- kept distinct per the house distractor-difference rule.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure NOT derived from neural crest cells
questions.question: The neural crest cells give rise to the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS derived from the neural crest). Melanocytes are neural crest cells that migrate into the epidermis and elsewhere.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS derived from the neural crest). Dorsal root (sensory) ganglia form from neural crest cells that condense alongside the developing spinal cord.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this IS derived from the neural crest). Sympathetic and parasympathetic (autonomic) ganglia are likewise neural crest derivatives.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this IS derived from the neural crest). The adrenal medulla is populated by neural crest cells that differentiate into chromaffin cells, distinguishing it from the mesodermal adrenal cortex.
explanations.E: Correct. The retina, along with the rest of the optic cup and optic stalk, develops from the neural tube (specifically an outgrowth of the diencephalon), not from the neural crest. It is therefore the one structure on this list that is a neural tube derivative rather than a neural crest derivative, distinguishing it from melanocytes, the two ganglion types, and the adrenal medulla, which are all genuinely neural crest in origin.

questions.learning_objective: State that the retina, unlike melanocytes, dorsal root/autonomic ganglia and the adrenal medulla, is a neural tube rather than a neural crest derivative.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.17 row 35 (e, remark: "Retina of the eye develops from the neural tube.")

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Normal vessel count of the umbilical cord
questions.question: The vessels of the umbilical cord are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. This understates the artery count; the normal full-term cord carries two umbilical arteries, not one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Although the cord originally contains a pair of veins as well as a pair of arteries, the right umbilical vein normally degenerates, so two veins do not both persist to term.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This reverses the true counts; the cord has two arteries and one vein, not one artery and two veins.
explanations.D: Correct. The full-term umbilical cord normally contains two umbilical arteries and a single umbilical vein, the left one, since the right umbilical vein degenerates during the embryonic period. This same fact is what Q52 tests, in EXCEPT form, by asking which statement about the cord is false (that it contains the ductus venosus).
explanations.E: Incorrect. The cord does retain a vein (the left umbilical vein) at term, so "no veins" is incorrect alongside the correct two-artery count.

questions.learning_objective: State that the normal umbilical cord contains two arteries and one vein.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.18 row 36 (d, remark: "Umbilical vein.", read from a torn/curved key page; letter column intact, remark truncated)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Category of fetal anomaly causing hydramnios
questions.question: Which of the following fetal anomalies may cause hydramnios (polyhydramnios)?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cardiac anomalies are not the standard mechanism taught for hydramnios; the classic mechanism is impaired swallowing/absorption of fluid.
explanations.B: Correct. Gastrointestinal anomalies that block the fetus from swallowing and absorbing amniotic fluid, esophageal atresia being the classic named example, are the standard taught cause of hydramnios (polyhydramnios). This is the same fact Q32 names specifically (esophageal atresia) rather than at the level of an anomaly category.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Musculoskeletal anomalies are not the classic taught cause of hydramnios.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Urinary tract anomalies (e.g. renal agenesis) reduce fetal urine output and so classically cause oligohydramnios, the opposite finding.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Nervous system anomalies are not the standard taught mechanism for hydramnios, though some severe central nervous system malformations can occasionally impair swallowing indirectly; this is not the classic teaching pairing tested here.

questions.learning_objective: State that gastrointestinal anomalies, not cardiac, musculoskeletal, urinary or nervous ones, are the classic taught cause of hydramnios.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.18 row 37 (b, remark: "Gastrointestinal ... polyhydramnios", read from a torn/curved key page; letter column intact, remark truncated)
field_notes.dup_check: Same underlying fact as Q32 (hydramnios <-> esophageal atresia/GI cause) but a materially different, non-overlapping distractor set (Q32 names specific organ anomalies; Q37 names broad anomaly categories) -- kept distinct per the house distractor-difference rule.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Origin of the nucleus pulposus
questions.question: Nucleus pulposus of intervertebral disc develops from the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The neural crest gives rise to peripheral neural and pigment structures, not to the nucleus pulposus.
explanations.B: Correct. As the vertebral column forms around it, most of the notochord regresses, but the segments trapped within each developing intervertebral disc persist and expand to form the gelatinous nucleus pulposus at the disc's centre. This is one of the notochord's few surviving adult remnants, and the standard fact examiners test whenever they ask what forms the nucleus pulposus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The sclerotome (from the somites) forms the vertebral bodies and the annulus fibrosus surrounding the disc, not the nucleus pulposus itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The somite as a whole contributes the vertebrae, dermis and muscle via its sclerotome and dermomyotome, but the nucleus pulposus specifically comes from the notochord trapped within the disc, not from somite tissue.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Ectoderm gives rise to the epidermis, its appendages and the nervous system, unrelated to the intervertebral disc.

questions.learning_objective: State that the nucleus pulposus of the intervertebral disc develops from the notochord.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.18 row 38 (b, remark: "Notoch[ord]", read from a torn/curved key page; letter column intact, remark truncated)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Germ layer forming the gastrointestinal tract
questions.question: Which germ layer forms the gastrointestinal tract?

explanations.A: Correct. The endoderm forms the epithelial lining of the entire primitive gut tube, from the pharynx to the anal canal, along with the epithelium of every organ that buds from it, including the liver, pancreas and respiratory tree. This is the same fact tested with respiratory-specific wording in Q13/Q25 and with an epithelium-specific option in Q48; here it is asked at the level of the gastrointestinal tract as a whole.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ectoderm forms the epidermis, its appendages and the entire nervous system, not the gut tube.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Paraxial mesoderm forms the somites (axial skeleton, dermis, skeletal muscle), not the gut tube's own lining.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Intermediate mesoderm forms the urogenital system, unrelated to the gut tube's lining.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Lateral plate mesoderm contributes the muscular and connective-tissue wall of the gut and the coelomic linings around it, but not the gut's epithelial lining itself.

questions.learning_objective: State that the gastrointestinal tract's epithelial lining is formed from endoderm.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.18 row 39 (a, remark: "Endod[erm]", read from a torn/curved key page; letter column intact, remark truncated)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Origin of skin pigment cells (melanocytes)
questions.question: Pigment cells of the skin (melanocytes) are derived from the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The notochord induces overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate but does not itself give rise to melanocytes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Surface ectoderm forms the epidermis proper and its appendages, but melanocytes are a separate cell population that migrates into it rather than arising from it directly.
explanations.C: Correct. Melanocytes are neural crest cells that migrate from the dorsal neural tube into the epidermis, where they come to reside among (but do not arise from) the surface ectoderm's own keratinocytes. Since the neural crest itself separates from the ectodermal neural folds, melanocytes are ectodermal in lineage despite arriving in the skin from elsewhere.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lateral plate mesoderm contributes to the body wall and limb connective tissue and to serous membrane linings, not to melanocytes.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The dermomyotome, a somite derivative, forms the dermis and skeletal muscle, not the epidermis's pigment cells.

questions.learning_objective: State that melanocytes are neural crest derivatives that migrate into the epidermis.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.18 row 40 (c, remark: "Meland[ocytes]", read from a torn/curved key page; letter column intact, remark truncated)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure that induces nervous system development
questions.question: Induces embryonic development of the nervous system:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The connecting stalk anchors the embryo to the developing placenta and later becomes the umbilical cord; it plays no role in inducing the nervous system.
explanations.B: Correct. The notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to thicken into the neural plate, which then folds to form the neural tube, the primordium of the entire central nervous system. This inductive relationship is a foundational fact of neurulation, and it is why the notochord is described as running immediately beneath the developing neural tube throughout the third and fourth weeks.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The hypoblast is displaced by epiblast cells during gastrulation and contributes to extraembryonic structures, not to inducing the nervous system.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The primitive streak is the site through which epiblast cells ingress to form mesoderm and endoderm; it is not itself the direct inducer of the neural plate.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The prechordal (prochordal) plate is a small area cranial to the notochord that marks the future oropharyngeal membrane; it is not the structure that induces the neural plate.

questions.learning_objective: State that the notochord induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.18 row 41 (b, remark: "Notoc[hord]", read from a torn/curved key page; letter column intact, remark truncated)

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure NOT of neural crest origin
questions.question: The following structures are of neural crest origin EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS of neural crest origin). Melanocytes are neural crest cells that migrate into the epidermis.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS of neural crest origin). The dorsal root ganglion forms from neural crest cells that condense beside the developing spinal cord.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this IS of neural crest origin). Schwann cells, which myelinate peripheral axons, are neural crest derivatives.
explanations.D: Correct. The dura mater is mesodermal in origin, unlike the arachnoid and pia mater, which develop from neural crest (together termed the leptomeninges alongside some mesodermal contribution). Dura mater is therefore the one meningeal/peripheral structure on this list that is genuinely NOT a neural crest derivative, distinguishing it from melanocytes, the dorsal root ganglion, Schwann cells and the arachnoid mater.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this IS of neural crest origin). The arachnoid mater, together with the pia mater, develops largely from neural crest cells, unlike the mesodermal dura mater.

questions.learning_objective: State that the dura mater, unlike the arachnoid mater and other listed structures, is mesodermal rather than neural crest in origin.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Week of intrauterine life when gastrulation occurs
questions.question: On what week of intrauterine life does gastrulation occur?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The second week is dominated by implantation and bilaminar disc formation, before gastrulation begins.
explanations.B: Incorrect. By the fourth week gastrulation has already been completed and neurulation and folding are underway.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The fifth week is well into organogenesis, long after gastrulation has finished.
explanations.D: Correct. Gastrulation, the formation of the trilaminar embryonic disc through the primitive streak, is the defining event of the third week of development. It converts the bilaminar disc into the three-layered disc (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm) that every later organ system develops from, and it is this same third-week timing that this exam bank's other week-3 events (neurulation, folding, somite formation) all build on.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The first week covers fertilisation through the early stages of implantation, well before the primitive streak or gastrulation appear.

questions.learning_objective: State that gastrulation occurs during the third week of intrauterine life.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Origin of the notochord
questions.question: The notochord is derived from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Endoderm is itself a downstream product of gastrulation, formed by epiblast cells displacing the hypoblast, not the source of the notochord.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The hypoblast is displaced during gastrulation rather than contributing cells to the notochord.
explanations.C: Incorrect, at least not directly by this exam's own convention. Although the notochord is often described in general terms as a mesodermal derivative once formed, the printed key attributes its origin to the epiblast, the population of cells that migrate through the primitive node to form the notochordal process in the first place.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Ectoderm is what remains of the epiblast after cells have ingressed through the primitive streak and node; it is not the source population for the notochord.
explanations.E: Correct per the printed key. Cells of the epiblast migrate through the primitive node and regress cranially as the notochordal process, which subsequently develops a lumen (notochordal canal) and finally solidifies into the definitive notochord. This traces the notochord's origin to the same epiblast population that, via the primitive streak more caudally, also gives rise to the general intraembryonic mesoderm.

questions.learning_objective: State that the notochord traces its origin to epiblast cells migrating through the primitive node.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure formed by lateral folding
questions.question: Lateral folding leads to the formation of an elongated:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Lateral folding pinches the flat endodermal sheet into the gut tube; it does not itself elongate the yolk sac, which instead shrinks as more of the endoderm is incorporated into the embryo.
explanations.B: Correct. As the flat trilaminar disc's lateral margins fold ventrally, the two lateral halves of the endoderm-lined yolk sac roof are carried together and pinched into a single, continuous, elongated gut tube running the length of the embryo. This is distinct from cephalocaudal folding, which instead repositions the heart, septum transversum and pericardial cavity ventrally.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The allantois is a small diverticulum of the hindgut/connecting stalk; it is not the structure elongated by lateral folding.
explanations.D: Incorrect. "Spinal tube" is not a standard embryological structure name here; the neural tube forms through neurulation, a separate folding process from the lateral body-wall folding that forms the gut tube.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The heart tube forms from the fusion of paired cardiogenic cords, a process associated with cephalocaudal (not lateral) folding bringing the cardiogenic area into the future thorax.

questions.learning_objective: State that lateral folding of the embryonic disc forms the elongated gut tube.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure somites do NOT differentiate into
questions.question: Somites may differentiate into all of the following except:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. somites DO form this). The sclerotome portion of the somite forms bone, contributing to the vertebrae and ribs.
explanations.B: Correct. The epidermis of the skin is a surface ectoderm derivative, not a somite derivative; the dermis, not the epidermis, is what the somite's dermatome contributes. This distinction, between the two layers of skin having two different germ-layer origins, is the same fact tested from the skin's own perspective in Q12.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. somites DO form this). The myotome portion of the somite forms skeletal muscle.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. somites DO form this). The sclerotome also contributes cartilage as part of the developing axial skeleton.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. somites DO form this). Somite-derived cells contribute connective tissue components alongside bone, cartilage and muscle.

questions.learning_objective: State that the epidermis of the skin, unlike bone, muscle, cartilage and connective tissue, is not a somite derivative.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure that is endodermal in origin (i)
questions.question: One of the following is endodermal in origin:

explanations.A: Correct. The epithelial lining of the gut tube is endodermal, since the entire primitive gut tube from pharynx to anal canal is lined by cells that trace back to this innermost germ layer. This is the same fact tested at the level of the gastrointestinal tract as a whole in Q39 and at the level of the respiratory tract's own endodermal lining in Q13/Q25, since the respiratory system buds from this same endodermal foregut.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tooth enamel is produced by the enamel organ, an ectodermal derivative, not an endodermal one.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The kidneys develop from the intermediate mesoderm, a mesodermal derivative.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Skeletal muscles develop from the myotome portion of the somites, a mesodermal derivative.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Bones develop chiefly from the sclerotome (or, for the skull and part of the face, from neural crest/mesoderm), not from endoderm.

questions.learning_objective: State that the gut epithelium, not tooth enamel, kidneys, skeletal muscles or bones, is endodermal in origin.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Origin of arteries, veins and lymphatic channels
questions.question: The arteries, veins and lymphatic channels develop from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Chorionic villi are placental structures rather than the germ-layer source of the vascular system generally.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Ectoderm forms the epidermis, its appendages and the nervous system, not the vasculature.
explanations.C: Correct. Blood vessels first form by vasculogenesis from mesodermal blood islands in the extraembryonic mesoderm and yolk sac wall. The same mesodermal origin holds for the intraembryonic arteries and veins that develop alongside this extraembryonic vasculature, and lymphatic channels, which appear somewhat later in development, share this same mesodermal source.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The amnion is the extraembryonic membrane enclosing the amniotic cavity, not the source of the vascular system.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Endoderm forms the gut tube's epithelial lining and its budded organs' epithelium, not blood vessels.

questions.learning_objective: State that arteries, veins and lymphatic channels all develop from mesoderm.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Temporary connection of amniotic cavity to yolk sac
questions.question: Amniotic cavity is temporarily connected to yolk sac cavity via:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Breakdown of the oropharyngeal membrane, when it occurs, opens the primitive mouth to the amniotic cavity, not a connection to the yolk sac cavity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The allantois is a diverticulum of the hindgut projecting into the connecting stalk; it is not itself the passage connecting the amniotic and yolk sac cavities.
explanations.C: Correct. The primitive pit, a small depression in the primitive node, deepens and extends ventrally until it briefly connects the amniotic cavity above the disc with the yolk sac cavity below it. This transient passage is the neurenteric canal, present only briefly during the third week before it normally closes again as the notochordal process solidifies. Because it runs specifically between the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac, and not any other pair of cavities, it is the standard answer whenever a question describes this particular temporary connection.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The vitello-intestinal (vitelline) duct connects the midgut to the yolk sac later in development, a different structure from the earlier, transient neurenteric canal.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Breakdown of the cloacal membrane opens the hindgut to the exterior at the future anal region, not a connection between the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac.

questions.learning_objective: State that the neurenteric canal is the transient connection between the amniotic cavity and the yolk sac cavity.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure NOT part of the intraembryonic mesoderm
questions.question: All the following are parts of the intraembryonic mesoderm EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS part of the intraembryonic mesoderm). The sclerotome is a subdivision of the paraxial mesoderm's somite.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS part of the intraembryonic mesoderm). The intermediate cell mass is the intermediate mesoderm column, one of the three main subdivisions.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this IS part of the intraembryonic mesoderm). The dermatome is the other subdivision, alongside the myotome and sclerotome, of the paraxial mesoderm's somite.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this IS part of the intraembryonic mesoderm). Lateral plate mesoderm is the third of the three main columns of intraembryonic mesoderm.
explanations.E: Correct. The connecting stalk is an extraembryonic structure, the precursor of the umbilical cord, that attaches the embryo to the developing placenta; it is not itself a subdivision of intraembryonic mesoderm. The sources of intraembryonic mesoderm (primitive streak, primitive node and notochord) and its own absence sites (the oropharyngeal and cloacal membranes) are already stated in the concept reused here as `main_concept`, which this item's own EXCEPT format tests from a subdivision angle rather than a sources angle.

questions.learning_objective: State that the connecting stalk, unlike the sclerotome, intermediate cell mass, dermatome and lateral plate mesoderm, is not a subdivision of intraembryonic mesoderm.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: False statement about the normal full-term umbilical cord
questions.question: All are true regarding the normal umbilical cord at birth EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this IS true). The full-term cord normally contains a single umbilical vein, the left one, since the right umbilical vein degenerates.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this IS true). The umbilical cord is covered by an amniotic epithelial sheath continuous with the amnion.
explanations.C: Correct. The ductus venosus is a separate fetal shunt vessel connecting the left umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava. It is located within the fetal liver, in the fetal abdomen, not within the umbilical cord itself, so it is not one of the cord's own normal contents. This statement about the cord is therefore the false one on the list, distinguishing the cord's own vessels (two arteries, one vein) from the intra-abdominal vessel the umbilical vein drains into.
explanations.D: Incorrect (i.e. this IS true). The full-term cord normally retains both umbilical arteries.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this IS true). The umbilical cord at term is approximately 50-60 cm long on average.

questions.learning_objective: State that the ductus venosus lies in the fetal liver rather than within the umbilical cord itself.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Day in development somites start to appear
questions.question: At which day in development does the somites start to appear?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The tenth day is well before the primitive streak and gastrulation have even begun.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The fifteenth day is during early primitive streak formation, before somites appear.
explanations.C: Correct. Somites begin to appear on approximately the twentieth day of development, with the first pair forming at this point. This is the same starting point Q34 tests with a different (day-numbered) option set. It is also the same day Q17 and Q29's somite-count-by-day arithmetic builds from, since three further pairs are added on each subsequent day.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The twenty-eighth day is well after somite formation has begun; by this point many somite pairs are already present.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The thirty-fifth day is later still, past the period when somites are actively being added.

questions.learning_objective: State that somites start to appear on approximately the twentieth day of development.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Fetal condition suggested by a case of hydramnios
questions.question: A case of hydramnios would make you suspect the baby may have:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Renal agenesis abolishes fetal urine output, the major source of amniotic fluid, causing oligohydramnios rather than hydramnios.
explanations.B: Correct. Oesophageal atresia blocks the fetus from swallowing amniotic fluid, so the fluid it would normally drink and absorb instead accumulates and produces hydramnios. This is the same classic pairing tested by name in Q32 and by category in Q37, now phrased as a clinical suspicion prompted by a hydramnios finding rather than as a direct definition question. It remains the single most commonly tested cause whenever this exam bank links hydramnios to a specific fetal anomaly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Immature (fetal) lungs are a feature of prematurity generally, not a classic cause of hydramnios.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An absent spleen is not a recognised classic cause of hydramnios.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Cardiac anomalies are not the classic taught mechanism for hydramnios; the standard teaching mechanism is a blocked swallowing/GI pathway.

questions.learning_objective: State that a case of hydramnios should raise suspicion of fetal oesophageal atresia.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Site where mesoderm is absent
questions.question: Mesoderm is absent in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Somites are themselves masses of paraxial mesoderm, so mesoderm is present, not absent, there.
explanations.B: Correct. The oral (bucco-pharyngeal) membrane is one of the sites where ectoderm and endoderm are directly fused with no intervening mesoderm. The cloacal membrane, at the streak's opposite end, is the other such site. This is the same absence fact this question cluster's own gastrulation concept states, that intraembryonic mesoderm develops between ectoderm and endoderm everywhere except at these two membranes and the median strip the notochord and neural tube occupy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The nephrogenic cord (intermediate cell mass) is itself a subdivision of intraembryonic mesoderm, so mesoderm is present there.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sclerotomes are the ventromedial, mesodermal part of each somite, so mesoderm is present there.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Dermomyotomes are the dorsolateral, mesodermal part of each somite, so mesoderm is present there.

questions.learning_objective: State that the oral (bucco-pharyngeal) membrane is one of the sites where intraembryonic mesoderm is absent.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Number of somites by the end of day 26
questions.question: By the end of 26 days, number of somites is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Fourteen somites corresponds to an earlier day under the standard formula.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sixteen somites corresponds to a day between 25 and 26, not the full day-26 count.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Eighteen somites is one short of the day-26 total.
explanations.D: Correct. Using the same day-by-day relationship this bank applies elsewhere (the first somite pair on day 20, then three pairs added each subsequent day, giving somite count = 3 x (day - 20) + 1), day 26 gives 3 x 6 + 1 = 19 somites. This is the same somite-count-by-day arithmetic Q17 and Q53 test with different day values.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Twenty-two somites corresponds to day 27 under the same formula, one day later than day 26.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Germ layers skin develops from
questions.question: Skin develops from:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own. Ectoderm alone accounts only for the epidermis and its appendages, not the whole of the skin.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Endoderm does not contribute to the skin at all.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own. Mesoderm alone accounts only for the dermis, not the whole of the skin.
explanations.D: Correct. The skin has a dual germ-layer origin: its outer epidermis, together with hairs, nails and sweat glands, is ectodermal, while its underlying dermis is mesodermal, arising from the dermatome portion of the somites. Because the question asks about the skin as a whole rather than a single layer, the correct answer must combine both contributing germ layers.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Endoderm plays no part in skin formation; the second contributing layer is mesoderm, not endoderm.

questions.learning_objective: State that the skin has a dual origin, ectodermal (epidermis) and mesodermal (dermis).

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structure that develops from neural crest
questions.question: Which of the following develops from neural crest?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The dura mater is a mesodermal derivative, not a neural crest one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The suprarenal (adrenal) cortex is mesodermal (from coelomic epithelium); it is the suprarenal medulla, not the cortex, that is neural crest in origin.
explanations.C: Correct. The neural crest gives rise to the sensory, sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia, among other peripheral derivatives. The dorsal root ganglion is a sensory ganglion, formed by neural crest cells that migrate to lie beside the developing spinal cord. It is therefore a genuine neural crest derivative, unlike the mesodermal or neural-tube options listed alongside it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The spinal cord is a neural tube derivative, part of the central nervous system, not a neural crest one.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The cerebral hemisphere is likewise a neural tube derivative, part of the central nervous system, not a neural crest one.
